title: Rashi's daughters
hookLine: tradition remembers them as learned; his grandsons began the Tosafist school

cards: Rashi had daughters, tradition says, and no sons. One answer to a legal question, preserved under his name, stops partway through for an apology.
The writer is weak and ill, he says, and can't hold the pen himself; his daughter is writing down his words.

That's how tradition reads it: a teacher in bed, and a daughter at the desk, taking down the law in her own hand. Through his daughters, his learning went on to the next generation, and the one after that.

teach.b: Tradition remembers their names as Yocheved, Miriam and Rachel.
We have very little written by them or about them directly, and that silence is worth saying out loud: what women in that world knew and taught was often never written down.
What we do know is the family that grew around them. Yocheved married Meir, one of Rashi's students. Their sons became great teachers in their own right.
One was Samuel, known as the Rashbam, who wrote his own commentary on the Torah and wasn't shy about reading a verse differently from his grandfather.
Another was Jacob, known as Rabbeinu Tam, a great teacher of law in France. These grandsons and their students began a new way of learning the Talmud.
They called their notes tosafot, additions.

Where Rashi explained a passage line by line, the Tosafists asked how this line fits with that one, in another tractate, and worked out contradictions, generation after generation, in schools across France and Germany.
Open a printed page of the Talmud today: Rashi on the inner margin, the Tosafot on the outer, the grandfather facing the school his grandsons began. And then there are the stories.
A popular one says Rashi's daughters wore tefillin.

teach.h: A STORY IS NOT A SOURCE.
teach.b: It's told and retold, but no early source says so, so tell it as a story.

What the sources do show is quieter, and real: a house where learning ran through the daughters to the grandsons, and a daughter who, tradition says, could take down her father's legal answers when he could not.

how: Students of the Talmud read each passage with Rashi on the inner margin and the Tosafot on the outer margin, and in some communities today girls and women study these same pages.

games.q: you are a grandson of Rashi. your grandfather explained the Talmud line by line. what do you and your students add?
o: notes that compare passages and work out contradictions.
games.why: they wrote tosafot, additions, asking how one passage fits with another, and their notes sit opposite Rashi on the page.

practice: Bring to mind a girl or young woman in your life, a daughter, a niece, a student, a neighbor's kid, and one thing she's curious about.
Picture handing her something, a book, a question, an hour of your time, a word that says her mind is worth training; if no one comes to mind, think of the girls you went to school with.
If you pray, you can hold her in your own words.
